newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Jewish family gets Holocaust funds.
newsitem.headline: Australian Jewish family gets Holocaust funds.

text.p: An Australian Jewish family on Saturday said it had made a successful claim for funds belonging to a Holocaust victim held in a Swiss bank.
The deal was made three weeks ago in Zurich between Sydney accountant Stephen Baruch and the Union Bank of Switzerland, Baruch told Reuters on Saturday.
"It is the first such deal in Australia and we believe, according to our solicitor, it is the first such claim in the world," Baruch said.
Baruch said he could not disclose the amount involved as the agreement with the Swiss bank was confidential.
The Australian newspaper reported Jewish community sources saying the amount, based on an original deposit of 600 pounds sterling in 1938, was now worth more than A$200,000 (US$154,000).
Baruch said his grandfather, Salem Buzyner, deposited his money in a secret Swiss account to protect his family's assets from the Nazis during World War Two.

The wealthy Polish mill owner made his secret deposit with the Union Bank of Switzerland in 1938 but during the war the family's fortune was dispersed. Buzyner died in Italy and his extended family moved to Australia.
In a search last year, Swiss banks found about 43 million Swiss francs (US$30 million) in dormant accounts possibly held by Holocaust victims.

Swiss banks have said they would publish a first list of pre-1945 dormant accounts on July 23, using the Internet and other media to spread the information internationally so Holocaust survivors or their heirs could come forward.
An independent, international arbitration panel will resolve the claims, according to a June statement from the Swiss Federal Banking Commission and a Swiss-Jewish commission.
Baruch said he believed his successful case will encourage other Holocaust survivors and the families of Holocaust victims.
"I imagine more people will ask or seek retribution and will be more confident of getting it because we have set a precedent," Baruch said.

Baruch said his personal case was successful because his family still held bank documents, which proved ownership of the funds. "We had good documents, bank statements, not many people have that and they may have to seek justice through class actions," he said.
Baruch said the Swiss bank had been very difficult to deal with during the three-year case. "I feel at last we have received some justice, we did not want the bank to get away with it," he said.
Hundreds of Australian-based Jews are believed to have lodged claims against Swiss banks.
